results.answer:
**Ruling:** Nothing happens to it. Under Blood Moon your Urza's Saga gets no lore counter and isn't sacrificed. It stays on the battlefield with 2 lore counters for as long as Blood Moon is out. It keeps the two abilities that chapters I and II gave it, and it can also tap for {R}.

**Why:**
1. **What Blood Moon removes.** Blood Moon says: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." When an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land "loses all abilities generated from its rules text" and gains the matching mana ability (CR 305.7, applied in layer 4, CR 613.1d). That removes the Saga's printed chapter abilities I, II and III, and adds "{T}: Add {R}."
2. **What it keeps.** CR 305.7 also says this "doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects." The two chapter abilities that already resolved granted "{T}: Add {C}." and "{2}, {T}: Create a 0/0 colorless Construct artifact creature token…", so those stay. The official Urza's Saga ruling (2021-06-18) agrees: it "keeps those abilities for as long as it's on the battlefield."
3. **No lore counter.** At the start of your precombat main phase, you add a lore counter to "each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities" (CR 714.3c). Your Saga now has no chapter abilities, so it doesn't get a counter and chapter III can't trigger.
4. **No sacrifice.** The sacrifice check only applies to "a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities" (CR 714.4 / 704.5s). Your Saga doesn't qualify, so it's never sacrificed. It simply stays where it is, still at 2 counters.

**Watch out for:** If Blood Moon leaves the battlefield, the chapter abilities come back. At your next precombat main phase the Saga gets its 3rd counter, chapter III triggers, and the Saga is sacrificed once that ability has left the stack (CR 714.3c, 714.4). Players often remember Blood Moon killing Urza's Saga right away, but that isn't what the current rules say.

**Sources:** Urza's Saga and Blood Moon (Oracle text and official rulings); CR 305.7, 613.1d, 714.3c, 714.4, 704.5s (Comprehensive Rules effective September 25, 2026).
lookups: Looking up Urza's Saga, Blood Moon · reading CR 305.7, 714.2, 714.3, 714.4, 704.5s, 613.1 · searching the rules for “Saga chapter abilities lore counter sacrifice”

**Ruling:** In your game (Opalescence first, then Humility), **Humility is a 1/1 enchantment creature with no abilities**, and **Opalescence is unchanged**: still a non-creature enchantment that keeps its ability. If Humility had come down first, the only difference is that **Humility would be a 4/4** (still a creature with no abilities). Either way, Humility's effect still makes every creature a 1/1 with no abilities.

**Why:**
1. **The cards:**
   - Opalescence: "Each **other** non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value."
   - Humility: "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1."
   - Opalescence doesn't animate itself (ruling, 2004-10-04). So it never becomes a creature, and Humility never touches it.
2. **Layer 4, type-changing (CR 613.1d):** Opalescence makes Humility an enchantment creature.
3. **Layer 6, ability removal (CR 613.1f):** Humility's effect makes all creatures lose their abilities. That includes Humility itself, since it's now a creature. But an effect that has started applying keeps applying in later layers, even if the ability that created it is removed along the way (CR 613.6). So Humility's 1/1 part and Opalescence's P/T part both still apply in layer 7b.
4. **Layer 7b, setting P/T (CR 613.4b):** Both effects set base P/T, so they apply in timestamp order. The later one wins (CR 613.7, 613.7a, 613.7d).
   - **Opalescence first (your game):** Opalescence makes Humility 4/4, then Humility makes it 1/1. **Result: 1/1.**
   - **Humility first:** Humility makes it 1/1, then Opalescence makes it 4/4 (mana value 4). **Result: 4/4.**
5. The official ruling on both cards (2009-10-01) walks through these exact two orders and reaches the same results.

**Watch out for:** Humility being a creature means it can be killed by creature removal, and it can attack (only if its controller has controlled it since the start of their most recent turn; Opalescence ruling, 2008-08-01). Other enchantments Opalescence animates also follow the timestamp rule: if they entered before Humility, they're 1/1; if they entered after, they're P/T equal to their mana value. A second Opalescence would change things again (Humility ruling, 2006-02-01).

**Sources:** Oracle text and rulings for Humility and Opalescence; CR 613.1, 613.4, 613.6, 613.7, 613.8 (Comprehensive Rules effective September 25, 2026).
lookups: Looking up Humility, Opalescence · reading CR 613.1, 613.4, 613.7, 613.8

results.answer:
**Ruling:** It's a **6/6** blue Frog with no abilities. Turn to Frog sets its base power and toughness to 1/1. Giant Growth's +3/+3 and the two +1/+1 counters still apply on top of that: 1/1 + 3/3 + 2/2 = 6/6.

**Why:**
1. Turn to Frog: *"Until end of turn, target creature loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1."* That sets power and toughness, so it goes in **layer 7b** (CR 613.4b: "Effects that refer to the base power and/or toughness of a creature apply in this layer"). It replaces the creature's printed 2/2, making it 1/1.
2. Giant Growth (*"Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn"*) and the +1/+1 counters both go in **layer 7c** (CR 613.4c: "Effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness… are applied"; CR 122.1a). Layer 7c always applies after 7b, so timing doesn't matter. Giant Growth resolving before Turn to Frog doesn't let the Frog "erase" it.
3. Official Turn to Frog ruling (2014-07-18): "Effects that modify a creature's power and/or toughness, such as the effect of Titanic Growth, will apply to the creature no matter when they started to take effect. The same is true for any counters that change its power and/or toughness."
4. Total: 1/1 → +3/+3 → +2/+2 = **6/6**.

**Watch out for:** If the creature has its own ability that pumps itself, like an anthem effect or a power/toughness-defining ability (for example "*/* equal to…"), that ability is gone, so it stops adding anything. Abilities and effects coming from other sources still apply (same ruling set, 2014-07-18).

**Sources:** Turn to Frog (Oracle + rulings 2014-07-18), Giant Growth (Oracle), CR 613.4, 613.4b, 613.4c, 613.7, 122.1a. CR effective September 25, 2026.
lookups: Looking up Turn to Frog, Giant Growth · reading CR 613.4, 613.7, 122.1a

results.answer:
**Ruling:** It gets **4** counters if you apply Hardened Scales first, or 3 if you apply Doubling Season first. You're the controller of the creature getting the counters, so you choose the order. Normally you'd pick 4.

**Why:**
1. Both cards are replacement effects, because each says "instead" (CR 614.1a).
   - Hardened Scales: *"If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead."*
   - Doubling Season: *"If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control, it puts twice that many of those counters on that permanent instead."*
2. When two or more replacement effects would change the same event, the controller of the affected object picks one to apply. Then you check again for whatever still applies (CR 616.1, 616.1e, 616.1f). Neither card is a self-replacement effect, so you can pick either one first.
3. **Scales first:** 1 → 2 (plus one) → 4 (doubled). **Season first:** 1 → 2 (doubled) → 3 (plus one).
4. An official Hardened Scales ruling (2023-09-01) confirms this: *"If two or more effects attempt to modify how many counters would be put on a creature you control, you choose the order to apply those effects, no matter who controls the sources of those effects."*

**Watch out for:** Doubling Season only works on counters put on by an *effect*. Its 2024-11-08 ruling says counters put on as a cost aren't doubled. Hardened Scales doesn't say "effect," so if the counter is part of a cost, only Scales applies and the creature gets 2.

**Sources:** Oracle text and rulings for Hardened Scales and Doubling Season; CR 614.1, 616.1 (Comprehensive Rules effective September 25, 2026).
lookups: Looking up Hardened Scales, Doubling Season · reading CR 616.1, 614.1

**Ruling:** Yes, your commander can still go to the command zone. Your "whenever a creature dies" triggers won't trigger, though, because the creature never actually dies.

**Why:**
1. Rest in Peace says: *"If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead."* So when your commander is destroyed, it goes to exile and never touches the graveyard. A replaced event "never happens" (CR 614.6).
2. **Command zone:** CR 903.9a says: *"If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. This is a state-based action."* Exile counts, so the next time state-based actions are checked, you can move it to the command zone.
3. **Dies triggers:** "Dies" means *"is put into a graveyard from the battlefield"* (CR 700.4). Your commander went to exile instead, so it didn't die. The official Rest in Peace ruling (2018-03-16) says so directly: *"abilities that trigger whenever a creature dies won't trigger because cards and tokens are never put into a player's graveyard."*

**Watch out for:** This covers every dies trigger while Rest in Peace is out: your commander's own "when this dies" abilities, Blood Artist-style payoffs and death triggers on your opponents' cards. It also applies to tokens.

**Sources:** Rest in Peace (Oracle text and 2018-03-16 ruling); CR 614.6, 700.4, 903.9a; Comprehensive Rules effective September 25, 2026.
lookups: Looking up Rest in Peace · reading CR 903.9, 614.6, 700.4, 614.12 · checking the glossary

**Ruling:** No, you don't win. The trigger still resolves, but your devotion to blue is now only 2. Two is less than the 3 cards in your library, so the win check fails.

**Why:**
1. Thassa's Oracle reads: *"When this creature enters, look at the top X cards of your library, where X is your devotion to blue. … If X is greater than or equal to the number of cards in your library, you win the game."*
2. Killing the Oracle doesn't stop the trigger. Once a triggered ability is on the stack, it resolves without its source.
3. Devotion is counted when the ability resolves, not when it triggers. The official ruling (2020-01-24) says you count devotion "as the ability resolves," and the Oracle "will be counted if it's still on the battlefield at that time." Devotion only counts permanents you control (CR 700.5). A creature in the graveyard isn't a permanent, so the Oracle's {U}{U} no longer counts.
4. When the trigger resolves, X = 2 (only your other permanent's {U}{U} counts). You look at the top 2 cards, put up to one of them on top, and put the rest on the bottom. Your library still has 3 cards. 2 ≥ 3 is false, so you don't win.

**Watch out for:** If the Oracle had stayed on the battlefield, X would have been 4, and 4 ≥ 3 means you win. The ability also checks your library size at resolution. So if you could get your library down to 2 or fewer cards in response, you'd still win with X = 2. That would need a draw or mill effect, which isn't in your question.

**Sources:** Thassa's Oracle (Oracle text and official ruling from 2020-01-24); CR 700.5 and 608.2h (Comprehensive Rules effective September 25, 2026).
lookups: Looking up Thassa's Oracle · reading CR 700.5, 608.2h · checking the glossary

results.answer:
**Ruling:** Electrolyze still resolves. The creature that's still on the battlefield takes 1 damage (not 2), and you draw a card.

**Why:**
1. You split the damage when you cast the spell, not when it resolves. Electrolyze reads: "deals 2 damage divided as you choose among one or two targets." Each target has to get at least 1 (CR 601.2d), so your split was locked in at 1 and 1.
2. When Electrolyze tries to resolve, it checks its targets. A target that's left the zone it was in is illegal (CR 608.2b). The creature that left is now an illegal target.
3. The spell only fails to resolve if *all* of its targets are illegal. Here one target is still legal, so it resolves normally. The illegal target isn't affected (CR 608.2b).
4. The 1 damage meant for the creature that left isn't moved to the other one. The official ruling (2017-11-17) says: "If Electrolyze targets two creatures and one becomes an illegal target, the remaining target is dealt 1 damage, not 2. You'll still draw a card."

**Watch out for:** If *both* targets become illegal, Electrolyze doesn't resolve at all. No damage is dealt and you **don't** draw a card (ruling 2017-11-17, CR 608.2b).

**Sources:** Electrolyze (Oracle text and rulings, 2017-11-17); CR 601.2d, 608.2b (Comprehensive Rules effective September 25, 2026).

**Ruling:** The defending player usually takes **6 damage**: 2 in the first-strike damage step and all 4 in the regular damage step. This assumes the 2/2 has no relevant abilities, like first strike or protection, and nothing else changes during combat.

**Why:**
1. **First combat damage step.** Your creature has double strike, so there are two combat damage steps, and only first strikers and double strikers deal damage in the first one (CR 702.4b / 510.4). Trample lets you assign excess damage to the player once every blocker has been assigned lethal damage (CR 702.19b). Lethal for the 2/2 is 2, so you assign **2 to the blocker and 2 to the player**. If you like, you can put more of the damage on the blocker. The 2/2 doesn't deal damage in this step because it has neither first strike nor double strike.
2. **The blocker dies.** It has 2 damage marked, so state-based actions put it into the graveyard before anyone gets priority.
3. **Second combat damage step.** Your creature still has double strike, so it deals damage again (CR 702.4b). It stays "blocked," but no creature is blocking it now. Without trample it would deal no damage (CR 510.1c). Trample changes that: when a blocked trampler has no blockers left, "its damage is assigned to the defending player… as though all blocking creatures have been assigned lethal damage" (CR 702.19d). So **all 4 goes to the player**.
4. **Total: 2 + 4 = 6.** The 2/2 never deals damage to your creature.

**Watch out for:** If the blocker survives the first step, for example because a separate effect makes it indestructible, it's still blocking in the second step. Its marked damage still counts, though, and CR 702.19b says to "take into account damage already marked on the creature." It already has lethal damage, so you can still trample all 4 over, and the total is still 6. A blocker with first strike or double strike would also deal damage to your creature in the first step.

**Sources:** CR 510.1c, 510.4, 702.4b, 702.19b, 702.19d (Comprehensive Rules effective September 25, 2026).
lookups: Reading CR 702.4, 702.19, 510.1, 510.4 · searching the rules for “double strike trample lethal damage”

results.answer:
**Ruling:** No, you don't have to tell them, and you get no penalty for staying quiet. Because the trigger would have helped them, your opponent normally gets no penalty either. At Competitive REL this falls under IPG 2.1, Game Play Error — Missed Trigger.

**Why:**
1. **It's their job to remember it.** IPG 2.1 says the player who controls a triggered ability is responsible for remembering it. It also says opponents "are not required to point out triggered abilities that they do not control, though they may do so if they wish."
2. **Staying quiet is never an infraction.** The annotated IPG 2.1 says you may stay quiet about an opponent's missed trigger, even one that would hurt them. You can't get a penalty for it, whether you stay quiet on purpose or just forget. That includes Cheating and Failure to Maintain Game State.
3. **The limit:** you must not **trick** them into missing it. Don't misrepresent the game state and don't pressure them to move on. As the annotation puts it, players don't have to help opponents beat them, but they can't trick them into missing triggers.
4. **Their penalty:** a missed trigger only gets a Warning if it's the kind that usually hurts its controller. For example, the Judge Academy (FTW) missed-trigger guide gives a Warning when an opponent's card draw is missed, but not when a player's own draw is missed. Since this trigger helps them, there's normally no Warning. IPG 2.1 also says judges don't step in on a missed trigger unless they plan to give a Warning or suspect the player is missing triggers on purpose.

**Watch out for:** Sometimes you need to know exactly when a trigger happens, or details about something it affected. IPG 2.1 says that in that case you may have to acknowledge the trigger before its controller does. One example is having to decide on blocks when the trigger could change an attacker's power. How the game gets fixed after a judge is called is set out in IPG 2.1's remedy section. I couldn't pull that exact text this time, so if it matters, call a judge and let them handle the fix. Don't negotiate it with your opponent.

**Sources:** Magic Infraction Procedure Guide 2.1, Game Play Error — Missed Trigger (annotated version at blogs.magicjudges.org/rules/ipg2-1/); Judge Academy FTW "Missed triggers" page (blogs.magicjudges.org/ftw/l2-prep/rules-and-policy/missed-triggers/). The Comprehensive Rules (effective September 25, 2026) don't cover this; it's a tournament policy question.

I couldn't find **Glimmerwing Sovereign** in the card database or in a web search, so I can't give you a verified ruling for it. It may be a misspelling, a custom cube card, or a card that hasn't been indexed yet. Please check the exact name or paste its rules text, and I'll give you the exact interaction.

In the meantime, here's how Blood Moon works. Check it against the card on the table.

**Ruling:** Blood Moon changes only **nonbasic lands**. If Glimmerwing Sovereign isn't a land, Blood Moon does nothing to it. If it is a nonbasic land, or an effect turns it into one, it becomes a Mountain. It then loses the abilities printed on it and can only tap for {R}.

**Why:**
1. Blood Moon's Oracle text: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." It affects only permanents that are lands and don't have the basic supertype (CR 305.8).
2. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type means "it loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type" (CR 305.7).
3. It keeps its card types, such as creature, and its supertypes, such as legendary. Per CR 305.7, setting subtypes "doesn't add or remove any card types (such as creature) or supertypes." Its name doesn't change either (ruling, 2020-08-07).
4. Abilities that work "when" or "as" the land enters, such as an ETB trigger or entering tapped, are lost before they can apply (rulings, 2020-08-07).

**Watch out for:** CR 305.7 says Blood Moon "doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects." If a different card gave Glimmerwing Sovereign an ability, it keeps that ability.

**Sources:** Blood Moon (Oracle text and rulings dated 2020-08-07); CR 305.7, 305.8, 613.1 (effective September 25, 2026). Glimmerwing Sovereign could not be verified.
